reference.source: RCOG and international guidance / standard gynaecology texts
clinicalPearls: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, causing a diffusely enlarged, tender, 'boggy' uterus
Typical symptoms are heavy menstrual bleeding and progressively worsening dysmenorrhoea, often with chronic pelvic pain
It classically affects multiparous women in their late reproductive years but is increasingly recognised in younger women with imaging
It frequently coexists with endometriosis and uterine fibroids, which can complicate the clinical picture
Transvaginal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging are the main diagnostic tools, showing myometrial changes and thickening of the junctional zone
Medical options aim to control bleeding and pain, including hormonal and intrauterine progestogen approaches
Conservative and uterine-sparing treatments are preferred in women wishing to retain fertility, with hysterectomy reserved for refractory disease
It may adversely affect fertility and pregnancy outcomes, which is relevant when counselling women planning conception
reference.pathophysiology: Adenomyosis develops when endometrial glands and stroma invade the myometrium, thought to occur through invagination of the basal endometrium along the disrupted endometrial-myometrial junction, or from metaplasia of displaced tissue. The ectopic tissue and surrounding smooth muscle undergo hypertrophy and hyperplasia under cyclical hormonal influence, producing a globular, enlarged uterus. Local oestrogen production, altered progesterone signalling, neuroangiogenesis, and inflammation contribute to heavy bleeding and pain, while distortion of the junctional zone and abnormal uterine contractility may impair implantation and contribute to subfertility.
additionalDifferentials: Dysfunctional or other causes of heavy menstrual bleeding
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound assessing myometrial texture and junctional zone
Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging for junctional zone thickening and extent
Full blood count to assess anaemia from heavy bleeding
Endometrial assessment or biopsy to exclude hyperplasia or malignancy where indicated
Assessment for coexisting endometriosis or fibroids
Histology of the hysterectomy specimen for definitive diagnosis
redFlags: Postmenopausal bleeding or intermenstrual bleeding suggesting alternative pathology
Rapidly enlarging uterine mass raising concern for malignancy
Severe anaemia from heavy menstrual loss
Pain unresponsive to appropriate treatment warranting reassessment
reference.prognosis: Adenomyosis is a benign but often chronic condition; symptoms frequently persist through the reproductive years and typically regress after menopause. Symptom control is achievable in many women with medical therapy, and hysterectomy is definitive when fertility is no longer desired.
pitfalls: Attributing all heavy bleeding and pain to fibroids and overlooking coexisting adenomyosis
Failing to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy in abnormal bleeding
Assuming imaging is normal because the uterus is only mildly enlarged
Overlooking the impact on fertility and pregnancy when counselling younger women
references: RCOG and national guidance on heavy menstrual bleeding
International consensus on adenomyosis imaging and classification
management: Offer the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system as first-line therapy to control heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhoea
Use other hormonal options such as combined or progestogen-only contraceptives, or GnRH analogues, to suppress cyclical bleeding and pain
Provide symptomatic relief of heavy bleeding and pain with tranexamic acid and NSAIDs
Correct iron-deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual loss with iron supplementation
Consider uterine-sparing intervention such as uterine artery embolisation or adenomyomectomy where fertility or uterine preservation is desired
Offer hysterectomy as definitive treatment once fertility is no longer desired
Refer for reproductive medicine input where subfertility is a concern and to gynaecology for coexisting endometriosis or fibroids
